full_judgment:
Anwarul Haque Chowdhury, J. : This rule arises out of an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against an order dated 2.9.90 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong in Money Suit No. 32 of 1990. decreeing the suit in part on admission made by the defendant-petitioner in his pleading in suit. 

 6. The plaintiff filed an objection to the prayer of the defendant for release of the attachment order and the plaintiff filed an application under Order 12 rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for part decree for Tk. 5,90,540.00 on the basis of the admission of the defendant in their pleadings. 

 7. The learned Subordinate Judge upon hearing the parties passed an order on 2.9.90 holding that the defendant may provide the bank guarantee as prayed for but ordered partial decree for an amount of Tk. 5,90,540.00 on the basis of admission in the pleadings of the defendant asking the defendant to realise the decretal amount within 15 days and further ordered the defendant to furnish the bank guarantee for the rest. Against which this revisional application was moved and the rule obtained. At the time of issuance of the rule the operation of the order was stayed by this Court which is now heard and disposed of by this judgment. 

 8. Mr. Rokonuddin Mahmud, the learned Counsel appearing in support of the rule for the petitioner having taken us through the impugned judgment and the other related papers in original from the records of the Money Suit submitted that the learned court below erred in law in holding that the defendant Company has made an admission in their pleadings in Court for the application to be allowed under Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure in view of the fact that no written objection was submitted by the defendant company in that suit at the time when the order decreeing the suit in part was passed. 

 9. It has been submitted that Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure provided that any party may, at any stage of suit, where admissions of fact have been made, either on the pleadings, or otherwise, apply to the Court for such judgment or order as upon such admission he may be entitled to, without waiting for the determination of any other question between the parties; and the Court may upon such application make such order, or give such judgment, as the Court may think just. It is the contention of the learned Counsel that under Order 12, rule 6 of the said order the admission need be made on the pleadings of the parties or otherwise and even if it is to be argued that there is some admissions made by the defendant in their written objection filed against an order of attachment, is not an admission in their pleadings because under Order 6, rule 1 "pleading" means only plaint or written statement and in the written statement of the defendant Company there having existed no admission and at the time of passing of the decree there having existed no written statement, the court misdirected itself in passing the order on the ground that the defendant admitted the claim partially in their pleadings, It has been further submitted that the applicability of the provision of Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure would be limited to the provision of Order 12 only. He has further submitted that in the written statement there was categorical denial made by the defendant Company as to any admission made by their Manager, Mrinal Kanti Dhar in written objection and he could not do so as he was not authorised to make any such admission and if he admits any the defendant Company is not bound by such admission. That being the position and the admission having been challenged subsequently in the written statement by the defendant Company and defendant Company having disowned the previous written objection filed by Mrinal Kanti Dhar on behalf of the Company, written objection filed by Mrinal Kanti Dhar on behalf of the Company while asking for vacating the attachment order, it could not be said that there was an unqualified admission made by defendant Company for it to be construed as an admission under Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure and even if there was an admission it was not unconditional as there also it was urged that the suit is not maintainable and there is no claim that can be decreed. That cannot be an admission to attract the provision of Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his contention he has relied upon the decisions reported in PLD 1966 (Karachi) 75, PLD 1952 (Dhaka), 137 and 25 DLR page 418. 

 10. Mr. M Fazlul Karim, the learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff opposite party in the Rule, submitted that the admission that was made was unconditional and, in fact, it was made even by the proprietor of the company himself subsequent to the written statement of the Manager of the Company, dated 15.5.90 and the subsequent admission was made by the proprietor in his application dated 4.6.90 and Mr. Karim referred to the said application in original, as on record. It is his submission that in the instant case, the provision of Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure is applicable and the Court has rightly passed the order causing no error or illegality or causing any injustice because the plaintiff in fact claimed much more than what is partially decreed and if the decree in part is allowed and eventually the court does not allow the claim of the plaintiff in full the defendant Company will suffer no loss but, on the other hand, the plaintiff who, according to the learned Advocate while carrying the fertilizer by his trucks and employed labourers had borrowed substantial amount from the market, if not paid immediately would be in very great difficulty but the defendant Company being very rich may pay Tk. 5,90,540.00 as a part decree. It will not affect them at all because on their own admission bills to an amount of Tk. 21.00 lacs are pending to be paid to the defendant Company by the BADC which is expected to be paid soon but the plaintiff has nothing to fall upon to repay the loan already incurred in the market. 

 11. In the instant case, the point to be decided is whether the provision of Order 12, rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure would be applicable in the facts and circumstances of the case for the Court to pass a decree in part on admission on pleadings of the parties in a suit. Order 12, rule 6 provided that admission made by the parties is to be admission made in pleadings or otherwise. Order 6, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure defines pleading to be the plaint or written statement. Written statement is not the same thing as written objection because Order 6 rule 1 does not include written objection to be a pleading. Written objection filed in an interlocutory matter during the proceeding would not be a part of the pleadings of the parties in the suit as such but we are of the view that if there is an admission in the said written objection it would certainly be regarded as an admission "otherwise" as appearing in rule 6. 

 14. In that case of the Chancery Division under report, Rule 6 of Order 32 of the Supreme Court Rule of England, which is similarly worded as in rule 6, Order 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the expression "or otherwise" came for consideration to substantiate the view that "otherwise" would also include even a letter written by the Solicitor of the defendant in the suit filed by the landlord for eviction for breach of a covenant of the contract, admitting breach of the covenant of the contract. The letter written by the Solicitor of the lessee to plaintiff Solicitor was not in any way related to any pleadings in court yet it was used as an admission under rule 6 Order 32 for decreeing the suit on the basis of such admission. Sargant, J. in delivering the judgment for the Chancery Division rejected the argument that the rule is confined to admissions made in the pleadings only and confined to rules 1 to rule 4 of the same Order, which rules 1 to 4 are also the same as in our Code of Civil Procedure, having found that the admission has been made "otherwise" 

 18. In the case of Wazedunnessa Khatun Vs. Daliluddin and others reported in 25 DLR 418 the same principle was reiterated to the effect that admission of the defendant must be positive, clear and unequivocal and the said admission cannot be split up. Thus, if there is an admission and in the other para there is a denial it cannot be said that there is an unequivocal admission and where there is an admission but it has been pleaded that the suit is not itself maintainable, then also no decree can be passed on such admission. 

 19. There is no dispute with the principles enunciated in the case under report but they are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case as in the instant case in the first written objection filed on 15.5.90, a clear admission has been made to the effect that the plaintiff after deduction is entitled only to an amount of Tk. 5,90,850.00 and they are willing to pay and willing to pay immediately through the court which was again reiterated by the proprietor himself, though in the written statement quite sometime after it has been submitted by the proprietor himself that it is the plaintiff who is demanding Tk. 5,90,850.00 though it was not due to him and as a matter of fact nothing is due to them and in fact the plaintiff has been over paid after disowning the admission made by his Manager in an application dated 15.5.90 but without withdrawing his own statement on admission made by him in Court on solemn affirmation dated 4.6.90. This written statement has been filed long after the court passed the decree in part. The court passed the decree in part on admission and at the time of passing of the decree on admission no such objection has been taken by the lawyer in court at the hearing that the admission made before by the owner himself or his Manager had no authority and when the court passed the decree on admission the written statement had not been submitted. 

 20. In the instant case we find that the order was passed by the Court decreeing the suit in part on admission and on unequivocal admission and passed when the denial, as made in the subsequent written statement, was not there before the Court nor any such denial was taken before the court. The decree on admission was passed, in our view, in accordance with law causing no error or illegality for this court to interfere in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction.
